title: 3 Keys To Being Consistent
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out three concrete techniques for teachers who struggle with follow-through despite genuinely wanting to be consistent. First, boundaries must be so sharply and thoroughly defined that students feel in their gut exactly when they've crossed a line, removing any gray area that would let a teacher hesitate to enforce a consequence. Second, teachers should make an explicit promise to themselves and their students to enforce the plan every time, treating their own integrity and their students' trust as the motivating pressure to follow through. Third, he recommends a daily ritual — a brief pause each morning to consciously decide to enforce the plan no matter what — arguing, citing the commonly cited 66-day habit-formation figure, that consistency becomes automatic once it is practiced as a deliberate daily decision rather than relied upon as willpower in the moment. He closes by addressing the common objection that a teacher can't be consistent about misbehavior they don't see, insisting that vigilant supervision is itself part of the job.
points: Boundaries must be defined so sharply that students feel in their gut, ahead of time, exactly when they've crossed a line.
Making an explicit promise to follow the classroom management plan every time leverages a teacher's own integrity as motivation to follow through.
A brief daily ritual of consciously deciding, each morning, to enforce the plan no matter what turns consistency into an automatic habit over time.
Consistency becomes effortless once it is treated as a genuine habit rather than something willed in the moment.
Vigilant supervision — putting yourself in position to see rule-breaking as it happens — is a prerequisite for consistent enforcement.
quotes: To be 100% consistent, it must be easy for you to follow through and hard not to. What follows are three keys to doing just that.
In this way, breaking rules is a choice your students know they’re making ahead of time and can feel in their gut when they do—like the drop of a roller coaster.
The soft pressure on your integrity, as well as the threat of your students losing all trust in you, is enough motivation to keep you from weakening and giving in.
Experts say that it takes 66 days to form a new habit. Make no mistake, consistency is a habit. Teachers who are consistent don’t even think about it.
Just sit and close your eyes. Breathe and calm yourself for 30 seconds or so, and then decide that you’re going to abide by your plan come hell or high water.
You must put yourself in position, both physically and with the detailed way you teach your classroom management plan, to be able to recognize rule-breaking the second it happens.
